
# Introduction

Three stories illustrate the central aims of this book; one sweeping and historic, and two small and personal. The first is the well-known story of Ukraine's Orange Revolution; the revolution, and other events like it in the late 1990s and early 2000s, contributed to a scholarly consensus that the risk of mass protest is incumbent's primary concern when considering the downsides of election manipulation. 

The second story concerns Marina Tarakanova, who served as deputy chair of a precinct election commission in the seaside city of Gelendzhik (Krasnodar Krai) in 2022. Tarakanova was helping to oversee the voting for the regional legislature in her precinct, Tarakanova was confronted (and filmed) by Ilona Grachevskaya, a candidate for office from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation. The video shows Grachevskaya accusing Tarakanova of hiding pre-filled ballots. Seated comfortably, Tarakanova refuses to move until Grachevskaya, the candidate, successfully gets the police involved. Upon instructions from an officer, Tarakanova stands, revealing the stack of ballots upon which she has been sitting; the officer rifles through the stack, showing that each has been pre-marked in favor of United Russia [@AdministrationGelendzhikGet2023]. The video drew widespread publicity, to the extent that the Central Election Commission felt compelled address the issue in a televised session. The Chair of the Commission, Ella Pamfilova, scolded officials, noting that the ambitions of any party, candidate, or official are not worth the risk. "It is not worth it, for this pretty young woman Tarakanova to risk her own personal reputation, along with the reputations of the election commission and the whole electoral system," Pamfilova said. Speaking to regional election officials, Pamfilova said "I want you to carefully examine why she did this. What motivated her? [@antonvoloschenkoHeadCECRussia2022]" 

In the case of Marina Tarakanova, the chair of the CEC need not have troubled herself overmuch to find a plausible answer. According to public records, Tarakanova's occupation was 'main specialist' in the department of mobilization work (i.e. the department which manages public resources for civil defense; Krasnodar Krai is a border region). For this work, her declared income in 2021 was ₽ 2,900,000: a very handsome sum for a civil servant in a region where the average yearly income was only ₽ 590,000. Her husband declared an additional income of ₽ 646,000 [@mariagridinaWhatKnownOfficial2022]. Despite their large joint income, the couple declared renting only a small flat along with ownership of two modest vehicles [@mariagridinaWhatKnownOfficial2022], though it is not unheard of for officials to omit luxury assets from such declarations [@szakonyiCorruptionCoOptationAutocracy2025]. As a municipal employee, Tarakanova's lucrative position---and possible future opportunities for enrichment that may exist in the civil defense sector---may have hinged on delivering satisfactory electoral results for United Russia, which dominates the regional legislature.
 
Whether she was indeed motivated by such patronage concerns will not be known, since---despite appeals to law enforcement by election observers, the KPRF, and even (tepidly) the ruling party [@antonvoloschenkoHeadCECRussia2022]---there has been no public investigation of the case. The chair of the regional election commission asserted that law enforcement was investigating the incident just days later [@antonvoloschenkoHeadCECRussia2022], however, no charges appear to have ever been brought against Tarakanova. Even in 2021, election monitors have for years complained to the courts in Krasnodar Krai that the regional Investigative Committee (i.e. the state prosecutor) has been quashing complaints of electoral crimes in the region [@CourtGelendzhikTires2021].

[Next add paragraph about regular people getting big fines for election manipulation.]

Other individuals, operating in different regions and perhaps lacking important connections, have not fared so well in the Russian legal system. In 2012, former precinct election chair Tatiana Arkhipova was convicted in court of stuffing 150 ballots in favor of United Russia's mayoral candidate into the ballot box, while destroying 150 opposition ballots. For this, and the subsequent forgery of the election protocol, she was fined ₽ 100,000. It is perhaps important to note that Arkhipova's case coincided with considerable turnover in the mayor's office; before her conviction, the candidate on whose behalf Arkhipova had tampered with the election was himself convicted of bribery, removed from office, and issued a fine of 18 million rubles. Three new mayors had since served in rapid succession [@HeadMoscowareaElection2012]. To foreshadow the argument to come, such disruption in the local patronage structure may have altered United Russia's willingness or ability to protect some local agents from legal consequences. In 2023, two teachers from Orenburg were convicted of falsifying votes and fined over ₽ 260,000---about six months' average annual wage for the region. Each year in Russia, a small number of election commissioners are convicted of falsification [@torochashnikovaBallotstuffingDoesntGet2021], while many more are convicted of lesser administrative violations of electoral procedure. While real jail time is almost unheard of [@torochashnikovaBallotstuffingDoesntGet2021], those who are convicted regularly receive substantial fines and/or suspended prison sentences.^[This is a status similar to probation; the convicted person must regularly check in with a probationary officer and avoid committing any other infractions during the period of a suspended sentence.]

Even when convicted individuals face light sentences, there are considerable downsides to becoming a convicted criminal in Russia. For instance, Article 351.1 of Russia's Labor Code prohibits those who "have or *have had* a criminal record, *are subject to or have been subject to* criminal prosecution" (emphasis added) for a variety of crimes from working in the field of education broadly; the listed crimes include crimes 'against freedom of the individual', a heading in the Russian criminal code which includes electoral manipulation. Since many of those who are pressured into manipulating elections are precinct election commissioners are teachers [@Forrat2018], exposure to the legal system also exposes these individuals to the possible loss of their career. Indeed, the law requires educational institutions to suspend teachers from work for the duration of legal proceedings [@CriminalsAllowedWork2015], depriving individuals of income for weeks or months. All this is further complicated by the legal requirement that workers in Russia maintain a formal record of their employment (the trudovaya knizhka, or labor book), which they must present to prospective employers. Records of disciplinary actions may be included in this book, which can complicate an individual's future job prospects. 

These examples are, of course, peculiarities of the Russian legal system. But they serve to highlight the intertwined complexities that can arise out of a criminal prosecution or conviction [@pagerMarkCriminalRecord2003;@kirkCollateralConsequencesPunishment2018]; these consequences can be expected to arise in authoritarian regimes, where courts often perform their ordinary functions outside of political cases [@shenbayhUndueProcess2022;@ginsburg_rule_2008] while serving to uphold regime legitimacy through law and order [@Whiting2017;@cheesmanOpposingRuleLaw2015]. Front-line election actors, who are typically placed fairly low in their patronage network, expose themselves to these kinds of risks and consequences when they participate in ballot stuffing, election fraud, and other forms of illegal electoral manipulation. Such exposure is not purely theoretical, as the examples from Russia---a relatively closed electoral authoritarian regime---demonstrate.

Stories like those of the two teachers who were fined a quarter of a million rubles each largely go unremarked upon, outside of the local press and the websites of determined election monitors. Among scholars of electoral manipulation and authoritarian stability, they have likewise received little attention. Instead, researchers have often---understandably---focused on mass protest as a downstream consequence of rigged elections. Such events are hard to ignore; they often involve great physical courage and resilience on the part of the protesters, provide compelling images for national and international media, and occasionally result in the downfall of authoritarian governments. Events like the 1986 People Power Revolution in the Philippines, Ukraine's 2004 Orange Revolution, or the 2005 Tulip Revolution in Kyrgyzstan, took a central place in theories of electoral manipulation. In these events, sometimes collectively called 'color revolutions,' post-election accusations of fraud contribute to mass protest, which in turn led to the fall of incumbent governments. The dramatic and consequential events highlighted for many observers the considerable risk that incumbents entertain when they manipulate elections. The cost of such manipulation is paid in lost popular legitimacy [@birch2011]; when an election appears sufficiently fraudulent, costly and potentially destabilizing citizen resistance can occur. Or, as others framed it, the use of election manipulation *reveals* the regime's existing lack of popular legitimacy, making opposition parties more confident in their chances of successfully ousting the incumbent through protest [@fearon_self-enforcing_2011;@Little2012;@Little2015;@magaloni2010]. Qualitative studies further developed the importance of opposition parties and civil society organizations in detecting and publicizing evidence of manipulation, in order to improve the likelihood of protest success [@Bunce2006]. This overall approach, in which electoral manipulation imposes a cost on manipulators in the form of costly risk to their tenure in office, has become a commonplace assumption in the literature on election manipulation.

In this book, I offer significant challenges to this this assumption, which I describe as the *regime-weakness model of electoral manipulation*. Instead, building on work by Simpser [@simpser2013], Rundlett and Svolik [@rundlett2016deliver], and myself [@Harvey2019;@Harvey2022;@harvey_manipulation_2016], I develop a *regime-strength* model of electoral manipulation in non-democracies. The regime-strength model address several questions that are puzzling under the regime-weakness framework: why does election manipulation persist in places where protest risk is high (as evidenced by the Color Revolutions themselves)? Why do incumbents often claim unbelievably high electoral results (like Belarusian president Aleksandr Lukashenko's ostensible 81 percent vote-share---with 84 percent turnout!---in 2020), if election manipulation is cheap talk that is likely to prompt costly protest? More significantly, it points toward more effective, though more difficult, measures of improving electoral integrity than reliance on the general public to act as a sort of natural immune system against rigged elections [@fearon_self-enforcing_2011]. To effectively improve electoral integrity, reformers and opposition actors must interrupt the machinery of manipulation by breaking the links between political principals and election-rigging agents.

The regime-strength model of electoral manipulation offers a pessimistic prognosis: the authoritarian incumbents who are best at rigging elections are also likely to be the best at surviving protest movements. The capacities and resources that authoritarian leaders need to engage the machinery of manipulation are the same as those needed to control society more broadly: extensive patronage networks, legal impunity for pro-regime agents. Incumbents in electoral authoritarian regimes are incentivized to build these capacities; moreover, the more incumbents face a credible opposition threat, the *more* incentivized they are to build such capacities. As a result, the regime-strength model makes predictions that at are diametrically opposed to those of the standard model; namely, electoral manipulation is likely to be more severe when protest risk is higher, and (if protests do occur), more manipulation is likely to be associated with quicker defeat for protest movements.

As a result, the model and findings make contributions beyond the study of electoral manipulation. Multiparty elections are a fundamental component of post-Cold War authoritarian politics [@magaloni2010political;@gandhi2009elections;@donno2013elections]. Elections have been found to have multiple benefits for authoritarian regime survival, including through the co-optation of certain electoral blocs [@gandhi2007;@gandhi2006;@reuter2015], the recruitment of effective politicians and agents [@greene_why_2007;@lust_okar2006], the revelation of information about political actors [@simpser2013;@Miller_2013], and the promotion of domestic and international legitimacy [@isikselVotingAuthoritarianElections2025;@levitsky2010]. Election manipulation is at the core of this process in authoritarian regimes. Authoritarian leaders use of a suite of tools [@schedler2002] to manage the uncertainty inherent in elections, which, after all, provide a focal point for opposition activity [@Knutsen2017]. To reduce the risk of electoral loss at the outset, authoritarian incumbents often deploy pre-election restrictions [@Szakonyi2021;@Bækken2015;@popova2012politicized], repression [@Bhasin2013], favorable institutional frameworks [@golosovAuthoritarianLearningDevelopment2017;@Birch2007;@Ong2018;@Tan2013]. 

However, these tools alone are often insufficient to achieve incumbents' aims. Electoral institutions that were fit for purpose years ago may no longer serve the regime's needs. An unexpectedly popular challenger may emerge. Economic conditions can deteriorate, damaging the incumbent's popularity. Even when pre-election rigging is working as expected, incumbents still need a mechanism to drive high turnout in uncompetitive elections. Finally, incumbents can use their control over resources and ability to break the rules to send signals of dominance that make other actors in society more apt to cooperate [@simpser2013;@gehlbach2015electoral]. To accomplish these goals, incumbents frequently turn to illegal forms of manipulation occur on or just before election day: vote-buying, voter pressure, ballot-stuffing, and outright falsification of results.

Consequently, the findings of this book improve our understanding of more than electoral manipulation alone (though this is already an important subject, due to the normative importance of electoral integrity). By identifying when electoral manipulation efforts are likely to succeed or fail, and what kinds of regimes are most likely to succeed, this book sheds light on major theoretical issues in comparative politics. These include, most directly, the stability of authoritarian regimes and the likelihood of further auctocratization. They also provide insights into the role elections play in democratization, and the have some implications for democratic backsliding.
 
## Existing explanations of electoral manipulation, and their limitations

For these reasons, election manipulation has long been understood to carry costs to incumbents that are fundamentally rooted in the loss of legitimacy. In an early influential study of historical electoral manipulation in Costa Rica, Lehoucq and Molina argue that the shift to more coercive and illegitimate forms of electoral manipulation, in combination with increasing targeting of more literate and densely populated communities "scandalized major sectors of the public," contributing to anti-government insurrections in the 1940s [@lehoucq2002]. The concept of the 'legitimacy cost' of manipulation (in contrast to its organizational resource cost) was developed at length by Birch [-@birch2011], who argues that "feared	loss	of legitimacy---domestic	and	international---is	the	most	significant	deterrent	to electoral manipulation" (p. 56). Drawing on World Values Survey data, Norris [@norris_why_2014] finds some empirical evidence of legitimacy costs along several dimensions. 

As the literature developed, events like the color revolutions figured prominently in theories of election manipulation and how it might be restrained. The role of legitimacy loss---and protest risk in particular---in preventing electoral manipulation has become especially influential in the formal modeling tradition. In some models, use of electoral manipulation is itself a signal of low incumbent legitimacy. According to this logic, some incumbents rely on manipulation to secure electoral victory, but---concerned about the potential costs of mass protests--some may instead opt to hold relatively fair elections. This approach carries a normatively hopeful message: strong opposition movements---those that are well-organized, well-funded, and enjoy broad public support---can effectively discourage incumbents from manipulating elections. As a result, the chances of democratic transition and consolidation increase. I refer to this hopeful interpretation as the "regime-weakness model" of manipulation.

```{r weakness-models, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Regime-weakness models of electoral manipulation and opposition protest", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("weakness_fig.png")
```

There are, generally speaking, two versions of the regime-weakness model. These are illustrated in Figure \@ref(fig:weakness-models). In the first, depicted in Panel A, awareness of electoral manipulation induces a loss of legitimacy among the public [@birch2011]; in other words, people are upset at violations of procedural justice [@cho_procedural_2016], and especially incensed if they believe the election was 'stolen' [@kuntz_more_2009;@tucker2007]. The focal point of the election allows individuals with diverse grievances to overcome their collective action problems and mobilize against the incumbent [@tucker2007]. An opposition that is politically stronger, a concept which includes a variety of subcomponents (e.g. underlying incumbent popularity, opposition unity, organizational and financial resources, etc.), in conjunction with this unifying moment of grievance-expression, increases the likelihood of 'spontaneous' mass protest. Regime weakness is implicated in this model as follows: When anti-incumbent grievances are more widespread, the incumbent is less genuinely popular. As such, it has an incentive to rely more heavily on electoral manipulation to make up for this deficit at election time. However, relying more heavily on electoral manipulation increases the risk of costly protest, a risk which is further increasing in opposition strength. As such, the more costly the expected protest (i.e., the stronger the opposition), the more an incumbent is disincentivized to rely on extensive electoral manipulation.

In the second approach, incumbent weakness is formally built into models of electoral manipulation. In this approach, electoral protest is modeled as a strategic decision by a rational opposition actor. The incumbent's likelihood of fending off a protest movement is equivalent to its ability to win an election fairly, in these models. Election fraud is a tool that allows unpopular incumbents to win elections; thus, when the opposition detects fraud it revises its belief about the incumbent's popularity downward. Election fraud can get the incumbent across the finish line in the election, but at the risk of signaling weakness to the opposition and prompting a costly protest response. This type of model predicts that opposition parties that are more capable of mobilizing protest, as well as institutional and contextual features that expose manipulation efforts, help deter election manipulation [@Little2012;@chernykh2015third;@Luo2020]. Figure \@ref(fig:weakness-models) illustrates this logic in Panel B. As the figure shows, both versions of the regime-weakness model imply that incumbents who wish to reduce the risk of mass protest can do so by reducing their use of electoral manipulation [@Luo2017;@Little2012;@Schedler2002;@Beaulieu2014a;@little2015elections].  


The regime-weakness model, while very plausible, produces some conceptual puzzles. Why, for instance, do incumbents claim excessive margins of victory (indicating massive falsification), if falsification is a signal of weakness? Under the regime-weakness model, the occurrence of post-election protest is *the* sign that informal negotiations between the incumbent and the opposition have broken down [@Beaulieu2014a]; the incumbent has manipulated 'too much' given the opposition's strength.  Given that the incumbent can choose how much election fraud to implement, why do we observe protest---what prevents incumbents from 'correctly' targeting the level of election fraud? And, perhaps most puzzling, why is it that most electoral protests fail to oust incumbents?

Scholars have, of course, advanced answers to these questions. Incumbents may claim unbelievably large margins of victory because that is what the opposition expects; perhaps it is the deviation from this expectation that triggers protest [@Little2012]. Manipulated elections that trigger protest may occur due to incomplete information, as both sides overestimate their chances of success in a post-election conflict [@smyth2020elections]. Likewise, over-optimistic opposition actors may produce the surfeit of unsuccessful protests that we observe.

Alternative answers to these questions are proposed in Simpser's model of electoral manipulation as a costly signal of incumbents' resources and capacities, which in turn influence other actors' expectations of the likelihood the incumbent will remain in office. Incumbents who blatantly or excessively manipulate elections demonstrate they have deep financial and organizational resources, and a willingness to break the law. In turn, elites, political parties, bureaucrats, and ordinary citizens expect the incumbent to remain in office in the future; these expectations lead to cooperative behavior with the incumbent, helping entrench their rule [@simpser2013]. According to this view, manipulation does not (merely) reveal a lack of popularity, but may also highlight other forms of resilience that can offset low public approval. A simplified illustration of Simpser's approach is presented in Figure \@ref(fig:simpserfig).


```{r simpserfig, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Simpser's model of electoral manipulation and opposition protest", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("simpser_fig.png")
```

As Figures \@ref(fig:weakness-models) and \@ref(fig:simpserfig) show, it should in principle be straightforward to distinguish between these two models empirically. In the regime-weakness model, electoral manipulation increases the risk of post-election protest; in the Simpser model, manipulation reduces the likelihood of protest (so long as it is excessive and/or blatant). However, empirical studies have not been able to conclusively settle this debate. Some studies have found that increased manipulation is associated with greater likelihood of protest, as the regime-weakness model would predict, while others have found no effect [@Hyde2014;@daxecker2012;@Hafner-Burton2016;@Lankina2017;@ananyevDictatorsSignalStrength2022]. A straightforward selection between the competing models of electoral manipulation has eluded the field, as a result.

---resources that can also be used to suppress post-election protest. I refer to this perspective as the "regime-strength model" of manipulation.







## Theory in brief



In this book, I propose an alternative conceptualization of how electoral manipulation relates to authoritarian regime resilience and protest, by integrating Simpser's argument with more recent work uncovering the principal-agent relationships inherent in electoral manipulation efforts. I call this the regime-strength model of electoral manipulation, and argue that it best explains the use and consequences of electoral manipulation techniques. Figure \@ref(fig:mytheory) illustrates the regime-strength model. 



```{r mytheory, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="A regime-strength model of electoral manipulation and opposition protest", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("mytheory_fig.png")
```

Incumbents in authoritarian regimes face the risk of revolutionary uprising as well as the risk of insider defection [@svolik_politics_2012]. These risks can be intertwined [@satoEliteCoordinationPopular2019], as mass protest can spark elite defections [@rioStrategicUncertaintyElite2022], and elites who split from the ruling coalition can use their own resources to stoke mass protest [@robertson_protest_2010]. When faced with relatively greater dangers to their position, whether it be mass- or elite-driven, incumbents in authoritarian regimes invest in various means of social control. To reduce the risk of being ousted, leaders will adjust institutions, attempt to purge elites or reduce their influence, shower benefits on cronies, and engage in repressive measures [@BuenodeMesquita2005]. They build parties of power that channel patronage resources and elite ambitions [@Reuter2009;@Reuter2010;@magaloni2008credible;@greene_why_2007], and co-opt their rivals using access to rents [@reuter2015;@gandhi2008political;@blaydes2011]. They censor traditional and social media in order to control the flow of information [@King2013;@Geddes1989;@lankina2020russian]. They fine-tune the independence of courts in order to optimize both political control and perceived legitimacy [@ginsburg_rule_2008]. And they build, deploy, and take pains to coup-proof the security forces to manage threats [@davenportMultiDimensionalThreatPerception1995;@Bhasin2013;@makaraCoupProofingMilitaryDefection2013]. The greater the threats faced by incumbents, the more they are motivated to develop these tools of control in order to retain their position [@svolik_politics_2012], all the more so, since loss of incumbency in an authoritarian regime often comes with steep personal penalties (e.g. loss of assets, imprisonment, exile, or death). 

In their efforts to govern and remain in power, authoritarian leaders must also contend with substantial principal-agent problems. Not even the most powerful dictator can rule alone; they require the cooperation of a vast network of actors, from their immediate subordinates down through a range of bureaucrats and mid-level elites, all the way down to ordinary citizens. At every stage, a subordinate's goals may diverge from those of the leader. The leader's closest allies are often the very ones who oust him; the very repressive forces which the dictator relies on to defend the regime from mass uprising may use their resources to topple him [@chinPersonalizationPowerMass2023;@svolik_politics_2012]. To keep the repressive apparatus loyal, the dictator must offer them spoils---but not too much, lest they use their resources to overthrow the boss [@draguPreventiveRepressionTwo2019]. Likewise, the incumbent may tolerate some level of corruption among his subordinates, but excessive corruption threatens mass unrest and also deprives the leader himself of some sources of rents; on the other hand, individuals have strong incentives to extract as much as they can from their positions of power. The incumbent may wish for judges to rule in his favor, but those judges may be eyeing the possibility that the opposition will take power, and hedge their bets [@Hilbink2007d;@helmke_courts_2012;@popova2012politicized]. Finally, the individuals charged with manipulating an election on the leader's behalf may have their own incentives to shirk, either to pocket their payments or to avoid exposure [@rundlett2016deliver;@Harvey2019].

Incumbents can mitigate these principal-agent problems through monitoring and punishing defection [@Ginsburg2008], though this can be difficult given the opaque information environment and agents' incentives to misrepresent their behavior [@tutumluParadoxAuthoritarianPower2021;@Boix2013]. Loyalty can be assured through shared characteristics between leader and agent [@svolikPowerSharingLeadership2009], like extended family ties, or shared revolutionary experience [@Levitsky2012]. More generally, incumbents work to ensure that their subordinates incentives are aligned with their own; that is, that they will be genuinely loyal out of self-interest [@Egorov2011]. A fundamental key to maintaining agents' loyalty is the power of expectations [@hale_patronal_2014]. If I expect the incumbent to be in power tomorrow, with the attendant ability to reward and punish, I am more incentivized to work on his behalf today. This, of course, becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy: the more agents are incentivized to work on the incumbent's behalf today, the more likely he is to remain in office tomorrow.

In electoral authoritarian regimes, election manipulation has a uniquely central role in this dynamic. One one hand, successful election manipulation is essential for setting up the expectation that the incumbent's time in office will continue indefinitely.  On the other hand, as with other aspects of authoritarian politics, the likelihood of 'successful' manipulation is itself subject to principal-agent problems [@rundlett2016deliver;@Harvey2019]. This means that, as incumbents respond to threats to their power by investing in the repressive apparatus, installing loyalists in key positions, centralizing control over patronage resources, and so on, they also reduce agency loss among election-manipulating agents. When those agents incentives are more closely aligned with the leader's, because of the leader's increasingly well-developed tools of social control, it is more likely that they will carry out their duties. In particular, as developed in more detail in the next chapter, I argue that centralize control over patronage networks and minimizing personal risks to agents (e.g. through compliant police and courts, or the absence of election monitoring) reduces agency loss among election manipulating agents.

This theory produces two direct hypotheses, and one indirect implication. First, it holds that electoral manipulation should increase in severity with opposition strength and with indicators of social control (i.e. low risk to agents, high resource control by the incumbent). Second, it predicts that increased electoral manipulation will be associated with a greater risk of *protest failure*---that is, with the likelihood that incumbents will defeat protest movements. Part of this effect, I argue, is directly attributable to manipulation itself. The more intensively an incumbent is able to manipulate the election, the more he signals that he has overcome a variety of principal-agent problems. This complements Simpser's view that excessive manipulation transmits information about the regime's capabilities. The more severely the election is manipulated, the more confident other regime actors will feel in the likelihood that the regime will survive the protest threat. In turn, they are more motivated to support the incumbent and deprive the opposition of support. Part of the effect, however, is non-causal---incumbents who are good at manipulating elections are also good at social control generally, making them more likely to defeat challengers.

Finally, this theory also offers an explanation for the mixed relationship between manipulation and protest that has been observed in the data. In this model, contrary to both the regime-weakness and Simpser approaches, there is no direct linkage between the degree of electoral manipulation. Instead, the occurrence of electoral protest is driven by the existence of the election and opposition strength, not by the degree to which the election has been rigged. Elections, at any level of integrity, create opportunities for contestation. The stronger an opposition group is---i.e. the more popular, unified, and well-resourced it is---the more likely it is to stage post-election protest. Whether electoral manipulation is associated with high or low levels of manipulation is contingent on the degree to which the incumbent has developed tools of social control. Where such tools are well developed in response to opposition strength, we should expect to see severe manipulation and a high likelihood of protest. However, when the incumbent has been less successful in developing tools of control, we are likely to observe protest in the context of a weakly manipulated election. The relationship that scholars find in their work, thus, hinges on case selection.

Yet much of the empirical record linking protest to electoral manipulation would seem to defy this prediction (albeit inconsistently). How is it that electoral manipulation can be a demonstration of regime strength, while still being regularly associated with protest occurrence? 


This debate has significant theoretical stakes for major questions of democratization and autocratization. The regime-weakness model of manipulation is optimistic; incumbents who wish to avoid revealing their weakness to strategic protesters may reduce or even eschew manipulation\textemdash an auspicious prediction that under-pins the idea of 'self-enforcing' democracy [@fearon_self-enforcing_2011]. However, if manipulation can indicate regime resilience, incumbents have incentives to both develop and deploy the machinery of manipulation---a gloomy prediction for democratization and democratic resilience. 

The answer lies in the frequently non-strategic (or at least not narrowly strategic) nature of anti-incumbent protest. In regime-weakness models, opposition behavior is narrowly strategic: opposition groups protest when they think they are likely to defeat the incumbent in the streets, and do not when they expect they will lose such a contest. Such models are well-founded in a rational-choice model of political behavior, which expects that individuals will be more likely to participate in collective action when they think the benefits (including likelihood of success in achieving protest goals) outweighs the individual risk of sanction [@Kuran1991, e.g.]. Beyond narrowly instrumental goals, a different model of protest holds that people are more likely to engage in contentious action when they have grievances against those in power [@gurrWhyMenRebel2015;@finkelRationalChoiceDynamics1998], a view which has been further bolstered by deeper understanding of the social psychological correlates of protest [@zomeren2013four;@VanZomeren2012].

Integrating this broader view of protest dynamics with the regime-strength model of electoral manipulation helps resolve the tension in the empirical data on protest occurrence, while also generating new testable hypotheses. Under the grievance framework, when citizens have many individual grievances against the incumbent, a highly manipulated election can serve as a coordination point for collective action [@tucker2007]. Crucially, protest initiation may be likely even if opposition actors see little chance of actually overthrowing the government




In order to reap the benefits of electoral manipulation, political candidates must rely on large, pyramidal networks of agents to affect the results (Auyero 2007; Hale 2014), raising the possibility that these agents may not always behave as the boss might prefer (Rundlett and Svolik 2016). Throughout this project, I consider a principal to be a national-level executive or party leader, while agents are the front-line individuals tasked with directly influencing election results by illegal means—the individuals who stuff the ballot boxes, buy the votes, and forge the results. As a result, I refer to principal-level effects as national, and agent-level effects as local. However, this model can be adapted to different electoral scales (i.e. the principal could be a mayor at the local scale).

Principals and agents care about different things. Agents care about access to patronage resources—jobs, rents, and other resources—that they can gain as a participant in a political leaders’ election-manipulation network. For example, a neighborhood broker who engages in vote-buying gains access to cash or other benefits (meant for distribution to voters) and may also be rewarded with a political position in the local administration through which additional rents can be extracted (Zarazaga, 2014). A schoolteacher pressed into service as an election administrator, as is common in Russian elections, may face pressure to participate in ballot-stuffing in order to preserve her job, salary, or benefits. The greater share of patronage resources that a political leader controls, the more attractive participation in her network is for agents. This increase in control over patronage resources acts as an incentive for agents to engage in electoral manipulation, increasing the likely severity of tampering with the election.

Political principals can benefit directly from electoral manipulation (Greene 2007; Magaloni 2006), since it improves their chance of winning close elections (Lehoucq and Molina 2002), and widens the margin of victory (Simpser 2013; Gehlbach and Simpser 2015). By contrast, agents perform their assigned tasks in order to remain embedded within a principal’s patronage network. To induce agent cooperation, principals in electoral authoritarian regimes tie access to the state and its associated rents to electoral success (Díaz Cayeros 2006; Lust-Okar 2006; Reuter and Robertson 2012; Reuter & Robertson 2015). This creates a powerful incentive for local agents to boost the principal’s vote-share by whatever means are available, in order to remain within the privileged network. 

However, if the principal appears less likely to control access to patronage due to electoral defeat or intraparty rivalry, her offer of post-election patronage will appear less viable, making it more difficult for principals to credibly commit to rewarding agents (Hale 2006). Following Hale’s (2014) conception of ‘patronal politics,’ I argue that a principal’s ability to credibly promise post-election patronage is contingent on patronage consolidation: the share of resources controlled by her patronage network, relative to those of potential rivals.  To clarify, for a patronage network to exist in the context of election manipulation, there must be continuous links between the political candidate (the principal) and the front-line agent in a particular territory; rewards and favors flow down from the candidate through a series of brokers to the individual agent in a particular local context. It is important to be clear about the distinction between the existence of patronage politics in a country generally, and the degree of consolidation of patronage networks. Patronage politics may be pervasive in a given case, but divided among many competing networks. In such a case, this theory predicts that it will be difficult for any one network to systematically mobilize large numbers of agents.

## From dissertation

When the last vestiges of the Soviet Union finally crumbled in December 1991, the dissipation of the old regime set in motion a process of decentralization within Russia itself: many of the newly-independent country’s regions sought to capture as much sovereignty from the center as they could swallow, to use President Boris Yeltsin’s famous phrase. While many of the old system’s levers of patronage and influence had passed into Yeltsin’s hands, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (KPRF) remained the only political party in the country that boasted a nationwide network of supporters, activists, and organizational infrastructure. These factors, combined with the economic pain of the transition to a market economy, resulted in the Communists’ victory in Russia’s first regularly scheduled legislative election, in December 1995, six months before Yeltsin himself was up for re-election. 

Yeltsin prevailed in that contest, despite Russia’s political fragmentation, a well-organized rival party in control of the legislature, difficult economic and social conditions, and approval ratings in the single digits a few months prior to the election. He accomplished this feat in no small part by drawing on the resources of the state and of allied business interests to manipulate media coverage, voters, and the election results. That an incumbent in such a challenging position could successfully manipulate an election is puzzling, since it flies in the face of dominant theories of electoral manipulation. Traditional theories of manipulation hold that it should be rare in just such a setting: where political competition is fierce and the risk of post-election protest is high. Similarly, more recent models that emphasize the staying-power of the leader—captured most clearly by approval ratings—drives local agents to participate in manipulation on his behalf; under this framework, Yeltsin’s dismal prospects after the KPRF victory in 1995 should have driven agents to play it safe. The outcome represented by Yeltsin’s victory in 1996 is one of the puzzles addressed by the theory presented in this manuscript: how can political candidates facing low popularity, internal political fragmentation, economic crisis, or other serious handicaps nevertheless produce enough electoral manipulation to win their elections?

Russian political history also provides a representative example of the second puzzle this project seeks to address. In important ways, the 2011 Russian legislative election was a mirror-image of the situation facing Yeltsin in 1996. The economy, while struggling to fully recover from the financial crisis of 2008, was growing. The country’s internal fragmentation had largely been arrested during President Vladimir Putin’s first two terms, in which regional authorities and wealthy oligarchs had both been brought firmly under the Kremlin’s influence. Six months from the election, Putin’s approval rating stood at 69 percent, and the ruling party—United Russia—was dominant in both the national legislature and in regional legislatures across the country. Despite these advantages, the ruling party suffered a significant defeat at the polls, losing 77 seats and its constitutional supermajority in the legislature. Even so, the results were tainted by widespread allegations of election manipulation, prompting a nationwide protest movement (Za Chestnye Vybory—For Fair Elections). The 2011 Russian election is an example of something close to the worst-case scenario for an electoral authoritarian leader: electoral defeat coupled with potentially destabilizing protest. That such a negative outcome occurred despite all of the advantages available to the ruling party represents the second puzzle studied here: how can incumbent leaders with strong states and deep resources sometimes fail to produce enough electoral manipulation to win the election and stave off mass protest?

This project offers a theory of electoral manipulation that explains both kinds of puzzling outcomes: ‘over-production’ of electoral manipulation by weak parties and ‘under-production’ by strong ones. In doing so it addresses broader research questions. Why does the severity of elections vary from country to country, within countries during the same election, and within the same territory from election to election? Why are different techniques used to bias electoral outcomes under different circumstances? And which actors drive that variation? I identity two explanatory factors that together account for type of electoral manipulation that is likely to occur in a particular case, as well as the severity. These are access to patronage resources on the one hand, and local risks to agents on the other. The appeal of participating in a rich patronage network draws agents to engage in electoral manipulation; leaders who have consolidated control over large patronage networks can generate more electoral manipulation as a result. However, local risks—public exposure, criminal penalties, and so on—make manipulation risky for agents.  These local risks are driven by factors like an independent and active media (which can investigate and publicize electoral malfeasance), an independent judiciary, and—most importantly—a large and active opposition party presence. These factors are generally not uniform features of a country, but tend to vary by locality. Just as democratic countries may have subnational authoritarian enclaves (Gibson, 2012), non-democratic countries may have pockets of elevated contestation and more active civil society (Gilley, 2010).

When local risks are high, agents are more likely to engage in forms of electoral manipulation that are difficult to observe and trace, in order to avoid exposure and punishment. These include tactics like vote-buying and voter pressure; agents who engage in these sorts of activities are difficult to monitor and track, since they take place at varying times on or before election day, and at places other than the polling station. As a result, I classify these hard-to-attribute methods as dispersed forms of manipulation. By contrast, techniques like falsification and ballot stuffing generally occur in the polling place on election day, making them easier to observe and for perpetrators to be identified. These are centralized tactics.

The model makes predictions for both the level and type of manipulation, summarized in Figure 1 and Table 1 below. In brief, when a leader’s control over patronage is low, manipulation on behalf of that party is relatively rare since inducing agents’ cooperation in the patronage network is difficult. It is least likely to occur in places where local risks to agents are high; if the leader controls enough patronage resources to attract election-manipulating agents, she is more likely to be able to do so in places agent risk is low. When leaders control a greater share of patronage resources, electoral manipulation increases in severity by tactic. In areas where opposition parties (in addition to independent media and courts) are weak, agents can engage in centralized manipulation like falsification of results. In high-risk areas agents are less likely to adopt centralized tactics, and more likely to engage in dispersed vote-buying and voter pressure. 

I test this theory using data from three country cases—Russia (2003-2012), Mexico (1994-2012), and Ukraine (2002-2014)—and multiple methods. For each case, I use election forensic techniques to identify potentially suspicious patterns in precinct-level election results and multilevel regression analysis to show how evidence of election tampering varies according to local and national political conditions. I also draw on field interviews and survey experimental results conducted in Russia, to help discriminate between possible causal explanations for the statistical results. More details on theory-testing are provided in the section on case selection and measurement later in this chapter.
